**ENTERPRISE SOLUTIONS PORTFOLIO**

**Enterprise Procurement Intelligence**

From request to payment, with full visibility at every step

**Complete solution guide**

An employee requests something, the right managers approve it, procurement selects a supplier, and the company tracks the order through delivery and payment. At every step, authorised users can see where the request is, who is responsible, and what happens next.

For companies, multi-company groups, trading companies, oil and gas, industry, banking, insurance and public organisations

# 1. The solution in one minute

**Enterprise Procurement Intelligence replaces purchase requests sent by e-mail, WhatsApp, phone or paper with one simple digital journey that everyone can follow.**

Every request gets a number, an owner at each step and a clear next action. Managers approve in one tap, buyers compare supplier offers side by side, logistics tracks the shipment, the warehouse confirms receipt and finance closes the file. Leaders can ask at any time: where is it, who has it, how much is it, and is it late?

| **Question**                    | **Answer**                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **What problem does it solve?** | Lost requests, slow approvals, no visibility, hard-to-justify supplier choices and no proof for audit.                           |
| **Who uses it?**                | Requesters, managers, buyers, logistics, warehouse, finance, management and administrators.                                      |
| **Does it replace the ERP?**    | No. It works alone on day one and connects to the ERP when one exists.                                                           |
| **Where does it run?**          | On the client's own servers or private cloud. No third-party licence is required.                                                |
| **Which languages?**            | Arabic (right to left), French and English from the first version.                                                               |
| **What makes it smart?**        | AI reads requests, quotes and documents, people check the result, and the system learns prices, delays and supplier performance. |

# 2. What changed in this version

This version fixes every weakness found in the commercial and technical review.

| **Weakness found**                           | **How it is fixed**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Scope too wide for a first version**       | Three editions. The Core edition covers internal and central purchasing, logistics tracking and closure. External sales, letters of credit and deep intercompany billing move to a Trading edition. Budget, supplier portal, integrity checks and ERP APIs move to Enterprise add-ons. |
| **No Arabic**                                | Arabic, French and English with right-to-left layout are part of the Core edition and of sprint 1.                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **SQL Server cost contradicts "no licence"** | The data layer supports PostgreSQL (free, default) and SQL Server (for clients who already own it). Migrations are written to run on both.                                                                                                                                             |
| **Approvers may not log in**                 | One-tap approval from e-mail, Microsoft Teams or WhatsApp through a secure, expiring link, plus a mobile web app.                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Manual entry of supplier quotes**          | Supplier quote link: the supplier uploads the quote through a one-time link and AI extracts the lines for the buyer to check.                                                                                                                                                          |
| **External sales blur the positioning**      | External customer journey kept as an add-on for trading companies only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Small vendor, sensitive data**             | Security pack, penetration test before go-live, source code escrow option, data export at any time and a clear support contract.                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Messy master data**                        | Import wizard for suppliers, items and cost centres with duplicate detection and AI matching.                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Ten sprints without a customer**           | A paying pilot client must be signed before sprint 3 and shapes sprints 3 to 9.                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

# 3. The example scenario: Atlas Group

To explain the solution simply, this guide follows one fictional group from start to finish. Atlas Group owns four subsidiaries in two countries and a central purchasing company that buys for all of them.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 1. Organisation chart of the example scenario

| **Entity or person**                           | **Role in the story**                                                                          |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Atlas Group**                                | The holding company. Its management sees every subsidiary and every request.                   |
| **Atlas Steel (subsidiary 1)**                 | A factory. It has its own approval rules, budget and currency.                                 |
| **Atlas Build, Atlas Warehouse, Atlas Europe** | Other subsidiaries: construction sites, central stores and a company abroad.                   |
| **Atlas Trading (central purchasing)**         | Buys for all subsidiaries, gets better prices by grouping needs and recharges each subsidiary. |
| **Sami**                                       | Maintenance engineer at Atlas Steel. He needs spare parts for a pump.                          |
| **Karim**                                      | Head of maintenance. He approves Sami's request.                                               |
| **Leila**                                      | Budget controller at Atlas Steel. She confirms the budget.                                     |
| **Nadia**                                      | Engineer at Atlas Steel. She checks that the offered parts are technically right.              |
| **Youssef and Ines**                           | Buyers at Atlas Trading: Youssef for local purchases, Ines for international ones.             |
| **Omar**                                       | Storekeeper. He receives the goods.                                                            |
| **Suppliers, forwarders, customs, banks**      | Outside the group. Suppliers send quotes through a secure link.                                |

A single company without subsidiaries is simply a group of one company: the same solution works for small and large organisations.

# 5. The three journeys

Every business need enters the app through one of three journeys. All three share the same purchasing core and the same tracking, so users learn the app only once.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 3. Three journeys, one shared core

| **Journey**              | **Who starts it**                                        | **What is special**                                                            | **Edition**                             |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| **Internal purchase**    | An employee of any company in the group                  | Approval by the employee's own company, then direct or central purchasing      | Core                                    |
| **Intercompany request** | A subsidiary that needs something another subsidiary has | Internal transfer instead of a new purchase, with a recharge between companies | Core (basic) and Trading (full billing) |
| **External customer**    | A customer, dealer or contractor                         | Commercial check, sales offer to the customer, customer order, then purchase   | Trading                                 |

# 6. Step by step: the complete use case

**Here is the full story of one request, in the order the app is used. Sami needs two mechanical seals and a bearing kit for pump P-204 at the Atlas Steel factory.**

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 4. The main journey in eleven steps

## Step 0. Sign in

Sami opens the app on his computer or phone and signs in with his company account. He chooses Arabic, French or English. The app shows only Atlas Steel, his company, and his own requests.

## Step 1. Create the request (Sami, requester)

- Sami clicks New request. He can fill in the form, or simply type: "2 mechanical seals and 1 bearing kit for pump P-204, urgent", or take a photo of the old part's label.
- The AI turns this into a draft with lines, quantities and a suggested category. Sami checks it, adds the datasheet and the required date.
- Company, department and cost centre are filled in automatically from his profile.
- He can save a draft or submit. On submission the app gives the request a unique number, for example REQ-2026-00418.

**What Sami sees next:** a tracker, like a parcel tracking page, showing "Waiting for Karim's approval".

## Step 2. Approve the business need (Karim, then Leila)

- Karim receives an e-mail and a Teams or WhatsApp message with a summary and two buttons: Approve and Review. He approves in one tap from his phone.
- Because the estimated amount is above his limit, the request goes on to Leila, the budget controller, who confirms that the budget is available.
- Each approver can also ask a question without sending the request back, return it for correction, reject it with a reason, or delegate during an absence.
- Every decision is recorded with name, date, time and comment.

**What Sami sees next:** "Approved. Sent to central purchasing."

## Step 3. Organise purchasing (procurement manager at Atlas Trading)

- The approved request appears automatically in the central buying queue, with requests from all subsidiaries.
- The procurement manager checks that it is complete and clear. If something is missing, he asks Sami directly from the request.
- The parts come from abroad, so the request is marked International and assigned to Ines. The app suggests the right buyer based on category and current workload.
- The app notices that Atlas Build asked for the same bearing kit last week and proposes to group both needs in one purchase.

## Step 4. Ask suppliers for quotes (Ines, buyer)

- Ines selects three suppliers from the supplier list. The app shows each supplier's past delays and quality score.
- She sends each supplier a secure quote link. Suppliers do not need an account: they open the link and upload their quote.
- For urgent local items, Youssef can use Quick quote with fewer steps.

## Step 5. Compare offers (Ines, with AI help)

- The AI reads each quote (PDF or scan) and fills in prices, delivery times, payment terms, Incoterms and validity. Ines checks each value next to the original document.
- The comparison table shows the best price, the best delivery time and the landed cost, which adds freight, insurance, duties and exchange rate to compare local and foreign offers fairly.
- Price memory shows the last price paid for the same part and warns if a quote is unusually high or low.

## Step 6. Evaluate and award (Nadia, finance and management)

- Nadia, the factory engineer, receives the offers for technical review. The AI highlights differences between each offer and the datasheet. She accepts two offers and refuses one with a reason.
- Finance checks the price, the currency and the payment terms. Management approves because the amount needs their signature.
- Ines records the award decision. The reason for the choice is saved for audit.

## Step 7. Place the order (Ines)

- Ines creates the purchase order from the awarded offer. If the company has an ERP, the order is sent to the ERP and its order number comes back to the app.
- The supplier confirms the order. Payment milestones (for example 30% advance and 70% on delivery) are recorded.

**What Sami sees next:** "Ordered from supplier B. Expected delivery: 14 December."

## Step 8. Track the shipment (logistics officer)

- The shipment moves through clear milestones: in production, ready, shipped, at port, customs clearance, in warehouse.
- Transport documents (invoice, packing list, bill of lading or air waybill, certificate of origin) are uploaded. The AI reads them and checks them against the order.
- If a milestone is late, Ines, Sami and the logistics officer are alerted, and the app recalculates the expected arrival date from past shipments.

## Step 9. Receive the goods (Omar and Sami)

- Omar scans the order QR code with his phone, enters the quantities received and takes photos.
- One seal arrives damaged. Omar records a partial receipt and a damage report. The missing quantity stays open until it is resolved.
- Sami confirms that the parts are the right ones.

## Step 10. Match the invoice and pay (finance)

- The supplier invoice is uploaded and read by the AI. The app checks that the order, the receipt and the invoice agree.
- The difference caused by the damaged seal is flagged. Finance waits for the replacement or a credit note before paying the balance.
- Payments are tracked until they are complete.

## Step 11. Close and learn

- The request closes only when delivery is confirmed, the required documents are present, the final invoice amount is checked and the responsible person confirms.
- Atlas Trading recharges the cost to Atlas Steel.
- The supplier's score is updated automatically (delay, damage, documents), which helps the next buyer.
- The full history stays available to authorised users and auditors, and can be exported as one audit pack.

## At any time: the CEO view

The CEO can open the request, or simply ask "Where is the pump P-204 request?" and get the answer: in transit, with Ines, 8 400 USD, ordered by Atlas Steel, two days late, now expected on 16 December.

# 7. Other common scenarios

| **Scenario**                            | **How the app handles it**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Urgent local purchase**               | The request is marked urgent with a reason. Youssef uses Quick quote with one or two suppliers. A shorter, still traceable approval path applies.                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Intercompany request**                | Atlas Build needs cement that Atlas Warehouse has in stock. After approval, the app proposes an internal transfer instead of a purchase. The warehouse ships, the site receives, and the cost is recharged between the two companies.                                                                        |
| **External customer (Trading edition)** | A contractor asks Atlas Trading for steel bars. The sales team checks the customer, Atlas Trading gets supplier quotes, sends the customer a sales offer with margin, and the customer accepts. The supplier order, delivery to the customer, customer invoice and payment are then tracked in the same app. |
| **Rejected or returned request**        | The approver gives a reason. The requester corrects the request and resubmits it, or the request ends. Everything stays in the history.                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Approver on leave**                   | The approver's delegate receives the requests automatically for the leave period. Every delegated decision is marked as such.                                                                                                                                                                                |

# 8. Request statuses

A request always has one clear status, shown in the tracker and in every list.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 5. Status lifecycle of a request

| **Status**                | **Meaning**                                    | **Who acts next**      |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| **Draft**                 | Being prepared, not yet sent                   | Requester              |
| **Submitted**             | Waiting for approval                           | Approvers              |
| **Returned for revision** | Sent back with a question or correction        | Requester              |
| **Rejected**              | Stopped, with a reason                         | Nobody                 |
| **Approved**              | Business need accepted                         | Procurement manager    |
| **Assigned**              | A buyer is in charge                           | Buyer                  |
| **Quoting**               | Suppliers are being consulted                  | Buyer and evaluators   |
| **Awarded**               | A supplier has been chosen                     | Buyer                  |
| **Ordered**               | Purchase order sent and confirmed              | Supplier and logistics |
| **In transit**            | Goods are on their way                         | Logistics              |
| **Received**              | Goods or service accepted, fully or partly     | Finance                |
| **Closed**                | Invoice matched, documents complete, confirmed | Nobody                 |

Each line of a multi-line request can have its own status, for example one part received and another still in transit.

# 10. Management visibility

| **Leadership question**         | **Where the answer comes from**                                     |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Where is the request?**       | Current status and full timeline                                    |
| **Who is responsible?**         | Current approver or buyer, and since when                           |
| **Which company asked for it?** | Company, department and requester                                   |
| **How much is it?**             | Estimated and committed amounts, in the original and group currency |
| **Is it approved?**             | Approvals received and pending                                      |
| **Is it late?**                 | Planned against actual dates at every step                          |
| **When will it arrive?**        | Expected date, recalculated from logistics                          |

Dashboards show requests by stage, delays, value by company and by local or international purchasing, buyer workload and supplier performance. Every view can be filtered by company, country, buyer, category, status, priority and date.

# 11. Connection with the ERP

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Figure 6. How the app talks to the ERP

| **Client situation**                                     | **How the app is used**                                                                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **No ERP, or no purchasing module**                      | The app is the purchasing system. Orders, receipts and exports for accounting are handled in the app. |
| **ERP with basic purchasing (Odoo, Sage, older Oracle)** | The app handles requests, approvals, quotes and tracking. Orders and accounting stay in the ERP.      |
| **Group with several ERPs, or an ERP being rolled out**  | The app is one front door for all companies, connected to each ERP.                                   |
| **Mature SAP with Ariba already in use**                 | Only the logistics tracking and visibility layer is offered.                                          |

| **Connection level**  | **How it works**                                                                            |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **1\. Standalone**    | No connection. Exports to Excel or CSV for accounting.                                      |
| **2\. File exchange** | Scheduled files: suppliers, items and budgets come in; approved requests and orders go out. |
| **3\. One-way API**   | Approved requests or orders are created automatically in the ERP.                           |
| **4\. Two-way API**   | Master data, orders, receipts, invoices and payments stay in sync.                          |

The app does not replace the ERP: it does no accounting, stock valuation or payroll. For a small company without an ERP, it can cover purchasing on its own until an ERP is needed. Some ERP vendors charge for indirect access when another system creates documents in their ERP; this is checked with each client.

# 12. Security, trust and continuity

- Company sign-in, strong passwords and two-step verification for managers, buyers and finance.
- Each user sees only their companies, requests and prices; suppliers and customers never see internal prices.
- Encryption of data in transit and at rest; every file scanned for viruses.
- Complete, tamper-evident history of every action: who, what, when, old value and new value.
- Automatic backups and tested restores; recovery plan agreed with the client.
- Penetration test before any external link or portal is opened.
- Source code escrow option, full data export at any time and a written support contract with response times.

# 13. Technology

| **Layer**          | **Choice**                                                                                     |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Screens**        | Angular web app, works on computer and phone, Arabic right to left, French and English.        |
| **Business logic** | Spring Boot (Java 21), documented REST API.                                                    |
| **Database**       | PostgreSQL by default (free); SQL Server supported for clients who already own it.             |
| **Approval flows** | Configurable workflow engine, no programming needed to change rules.                           |
| **AI**             | Python services running on the client's servers for reading documents and answering questions. |
| **Files**          | Secure file storage with versions.                                                             |
| **ERP link**       | Dedicated integration layer with retries, no duplicates and a daily reconciliation report.     |
| **Hosting**        | Client servers or private cloud, using containers.                                             |

# 14. Editions and pricing logic

| **Edition**            | **Content**                                                                                                                                                                                    | **For whom**                       |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| **Core**               | Requests, approvals, central buying queue, quotes and comparison, orders, logistics tracking, receipt, invoice matching, closure, dashboards, file exchange with the ERP, core smart features. | Any company or group               |
| **Trading add-on**     | External customer journey, sales offers, customer orders, full intercompany billing, letters of credit.                                                                                        | Trading and distribution companies |
| **Enterprise add-ons** | Budget control, supplier portal, integrity alerts, Ask the app, savings ledger, bottleneck heatmap, exchange-rate exposure, ERP APIs, high availability.                                       | Large groups                       |

Requesters and approvers are free. The client pays for buyers, logistics, finance and administrators, as a yearly subscription or a perpetual licence with annual maintenance. Amounts are given in the financial offer.

# Glossary

| **Term**               | **Meaning**                                                                         |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Request**            | A need for goods or a service, written in the app with a unique number.             |
| **Quote**              | A supplier's price offer.                                                           |
| **Purchase order**     | The official order sent to the supplier.                                            |
| **Landed cost**        | Total cost of goods delivered: price, freight, insurance, duties and exchange rate. |
| **Incoterms**          | International rules that say who pays for and handles transport and risk.           |
| **Central purchasing** | The company or team that buys for all companies of a group.                         |
| **Recharge**           | Passing the cost of a central purchase back to the subsidiary that needed it.       |
| **Three-way match**    | Checking that the order, the receipt and the invoice agree.                         |
| **ERP**                | The company's main management system for accounting, stock and payments.            |

**One request, one number, one owner at each step, and an immediate answer to "where is my purchase?".**
